title: What you think about often
hook: whatever one thinks about often, the mind inclines that way (MN 19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the honeyball, Mahakaccana's map of how one sight spreads into endless thoughts. Your line: the thoughts multiply.

Walk the same way across a lawn every day for a month, and you'll make a path. Nobody planned it. Nobody poured concrete. The grass just gave up where your feet kept landing, and now everyone walks that way without thinking. In MN 19, the Buddha says the mind works like that lawn, and he learned it by watching his own mind before his awakening.
screen: `THE SAME WAY ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `A PATH NOBODY PLANNED.`

segments.voice: MN 19, the Dvedhavitakka, the discourse on two kinds of thought. Before his awakening, the Buddha says, he divided his thoughts into two piles. On one side: thoughts of sense desire, ill will and cruelty. On the other: thoughts of renunciation, goodwill and non-cruelty. When one from the first pile arose, he noticed it plainly: this leads to my own harm, to others' harm, to both; it obstructs wisdom. And as he noticed, it faded. Then comes the sentence. Whatever a monk keeps thinking about and pondering, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Think often of ill will, and the mind leans toward ill will. Think often of goodwill, and it leans toward goodwill. Then a picture from farm life. In the last month of the rainy season, when the crops are thick, a cowherd has to watch his cows constantly, tapping and checking them with a stick to keep them out of the crops, because he can see the trouble coming if they get in. But in the last month of the hot season, with the harvest in, he can sit at the foot of a tree, or out in the open, and only needs to remember: there are the cows. At first the work is watchful. Later, the mind leans the right way on its own, and you can rest. The Dhammapada opens on the same ground, in Max Müller's translation: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought.”
screen: `TWO PILES OF THOUGHTS.` · `THE MIND INCLINES THAT WAY.` · `THE COWHERD BEFORE AND AFTER HARVEST.` · `ALL THAT WE ARE.` · then, large: `THE MIND INCLINES.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing to think about on purpose, a person you're grateful for, a kindness someone showed you, a place that calms you, and let it fill the sit. When the mind wanders, and it will, walk it back without scolding. One more step on the same spot of lawn.
Vitakka, thought. Whatever the mind keeps returning to, it starts to lean toward.
Your line: the mind inclines. A path across the lawn is made one step at a time. Day four hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist practitioners cultivate wholesome thoughts deliberately, for example through loving-kindness practice or recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, on the understanding that repeated thoughts shape the mind.

fork.setup: the crops are harvested and the fields are bare. what does the cowherd in MN 19 need to do?
options: sit under a tree and just remember: there are the cows
fork.reveal: with no crops at risk, mindfulness is enough. the Buddha uses it for a mind that already leans toward the good.

original.note: Pali vitakka: thought, thinking; MN 19 is the dvedhā-vitakka, thoughts split in two.

trapdoor: what it means: whatever you think about often, the mind starts leaning that way, for good or ill.
what a scholar hears: dvedhā-vitakka means thought divided in two; the cowherd image moves from watchful restraint to easy mindfulness as the mind's inclination changes.
recall: a barren, stony place in the heart

chat.says: Does it really matter what I let myself think about all day?
options: MN 19 says whatever you keep thinking about becomes the way your mind leans.
Not really; only your actions count, and thoughts pass without a trace.
Only if you say the thoughts out loud; silent thinking leaves no mark.
chat.meaning: MN 19: whatever one keeps thinking about and pondering becomes the inclination of the mind, toward ill will or toward goodwill.
